title: Administration and Finance of the East India Company
yearNote: Submitted 15 May 1915 for the M.A. degree, Columbia University.
summary: This was Ambedkar's M.A. thesis at Columbia University in New York. It explains how the British East India Company was run and how it raised and spent money while it ruled parts of India. It stayed unpublished until the Government of Maharashtra printed it in BAWS Vol. 6 (1989).
whyItMatters: It is his first long piece of academic research and shows his early interest in how money and government shape the lives of ordinary Indians.

physical.holder: Columbia University (New York)
physical.note: BAWS Vol. 6 says the dissertation is in Columbia University's 'ownership and possession'; a copy was obtained from Columbia by Dr. Frank F. Conlon (University of Washington) and given to Vasant Moon in 1979.

title: Ancient Indian Commerce
altTitles: Commercial Relations of India in the Middle East
Commercial Relations of India in the Middle Ages
India on the Eve of the Crown Government
yearNote: BAWS Vol. 12 prints a facsimile of his handwriting "during his student-days in America in the year 1915-16" from these pages. Frances Pritchett's timeline (citing Keer) says he presented a thesis called "Ancient Indian Commerce" for his 1915 M.A.; BAWS Vol. 6 instead prints "Administration and Finance of the East India Company" as the 1915 M.A. thesis. The sources disagree.
summary: Three handwritten essays on India's trade with the Roman world and the Middle East, trade in the Middle Ages and the rise of Islam, and India just before the British Crown took over in 1858. Some pages are missing, and the editors had to supply one title.
whyItMatters: They show the young student studying India's place in world history and trade, long before he became a political leader.

title: The National Dividend of India: A Historic and Analytical Study
yearNote: Offered at Columbia in 1916 (Keer, via Pritchett). Revised and published in London in 1925 as "The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India"; Columbia formally awarded the Ph.D. on 8 June 1927 according to his transcript (Pritchett). Other sources give other dates.
summary: This was the doctoral research Ambedkar did at Columbia University. He later reworked it into the book "The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India" (1925), and Columbia then awarded him the Ph.D.
whyItMatters: It grew into his book on how money was shared between British India's central and provincial governments, and it earned him his Columbia Ph.D.

title: Castes in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development
yearNote: Read on 9 May 1916 at Prof. A. A. Goldenweiser's anthropology seminar, Columbia University; printed in Indian Antiquary, May 1917 (Vol. XLI, as given in BAWS).
summary: A student paper that asks how caste began and how it keeps itself going. Ambedkar argues that caste is kept alive mainly by forbidding marriage outside the group (endogamy), and by customs such as child marriage and enforced widowhood that serve that purpose.
whyItMatters: It is his first published work and the starting point of a lifetime of thinking about caste.

online.label: Columbia University (Frances Pritchett) – edited text
Internet Archive – pamphlet reprint (Patrika Publications, Jullundur)

title: Small Holdings in India and Their Remedies
yearNote: Journal of the Indian Economic Society, Vol. I, 1918.
summary: An economics paper about Indian farms that were split into tiny plots. Ambedkar argues that making farms bigger is not enough; the real cure is industrialisation, which would take surplus workers off the land.
whyItMatters: It shows him as a trained economist who linked rural poverty to the need for industry.

title: Mr. Russell and the Reconstruction of Society
yearNote: Review of Bertrand Russell's "Principles of Social Reconstruction"; BAWS gives the Journal of the Indian Economic Society, Vol. I, 1918. Pritchett's timeline names the "Journal of Indian Economics (1,1)".
summary: A book review of Bertrand Russell's ideas on how society should be rebuilt after the First World War. Ambedkar discusses Russell's view that people act from impulses and asks how institutions can be changed.
whyItMatters: It shows the wide reading of the young scholar and his early interest in social change.

title: Provincial Decentralization of Imperial Finance in British India (M.Sc. thesis)
altTitles: The Provincial Decentralisation of Imperial Finance in India
yearNote: M.Sc. (Economics), London School of Economics. LSE's archivist says that on returning in 1920 he applied to complete his master's with a thesis titled "The Provincial Decentralisation of Imperial Finance in India". Pritchett's timeline dates the M.Sc. thesis to 1922; other sources say 1921.
summary: Ambedkar's master's thesis at the London School of Economics, about how the British government in India handed some money powers to the provinces. Its subject is close to his 1925 book on provincial finance, but the thesis itself has not been printed as a separate text.
whyItMatters: It is part of the academic record that made him one of the best-qualified economists of his time.

physical.holder: LSE Library Archives / University of London
physical.note: LSE's archivist describes Ambedkar's student file at LSE. Whether a bound copy of the M.Sc. thesis survives is not stated online.

title: The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and Its Solution
altTitles: History of Indian Currency and Banking, Vol. 1 (1947 edition)
yearNote: Doctoral thesis, University of London (LSE): submitted March 1923, resubmitted August 1923, accepted November 1923 (LSE archivist); published by P. S. King & Son, London, 1923. Reissued in 1947 as "History of Indian Currency and Banking, Vol. 1".
summary: A history of Indian money from the silver standard to the "gold exchange standard". Ambedkar criticises the gold exchange standard, under which the government could issue rupees at its discretion, and argues for a return to a gold standard with a fixed limit on the issue of rupees so that prices stay stable.
whyItMatters: It won him the D.Sc. from the University of London and is still cited in debates about Indian monetary history.

online.label: Internet Archive – 1923 P. S. King edition (Digital Library of India scan)
Internet Archive – History of Indian Currency and Banking (1947)

title: The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India: A Study in the Provincial Decentralization of Imperial Finance
yearNote: P. S. King & Son, London, 1925, with a foreword by Prof. Edwin R. A. Seligman of Columbia. Based on his Columbia doctoral research (see "The National Dividend of India"). Pritchett's 1920s page also calls it his "London School of Economics M.A. thesis" — the sources are not consistent.
summary: This book traces how the provinces of British India came to have their own finances: from the old centralised "Imperial System", through budgets by assignments and by shared revenues, to the changes made by the Government of India Act, 1919, which Ambedkar criticises.
whyItMatters: It was his Columbia Ph.D. work and an early, detailed study of Indian public finance and federalism.

online.label: Internet Archive – 1925 P. S. King edition

title: Statement of Evidence and Oral Evidence before the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance
yearNote: Written statement in reply to the Commission's questionnaire; oral evidence on 15 December 1925 (printed in the Commission's Report, Vols. II and IV, 1926).
summary: Ambedkar gave written and spoken evidence to a British commission on India's currency. He argued against the "gold exchange standard" and for a system that would keep prices steady.
whyItMatters: It shows him using his economics to influence official policy soon after finishing his doctorate.

online.label: Internet Archive – Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, Vol. IV, Minutes of Evidence (1926)

title: The Present Problem in Indian Currency (I and II)
yearNote: The Servant of India, 1 April and 16 April 1925.
summary: Two newspaper articles on the debate over whether the rupee should be fixed at 1 shilling 4 pence or 1 shilling 6 pence. Ambedkar explains what each choice would mean for prices and for ordinary people.
whyItMatters: They show him explaining hard economics to the public.

title: Review: Indian Currency and Exchange, by H. L. Chablani
yearNote: The Servant of India, 25 June 1925.
summary: A short and sharp review of a book on Indian currency. Ambedkar finds it thin on information and explanation.
whyItMatters: One of his few book reviews, showing his standards as an economist.

title: Review: Report of the Taxation Enquiry Committee, 1926
yearNote: The Servant of India, Vol. IX, No. 13, 29 April 1926.
summary: Ambedkar reviews an official report on India's tax system and comments on how committees are used to study policy.
whyItMatters: It shows his continuing work on public finance and taxation.

title: Foreword to "Commodity Exchanges" by P. G. Salvi
yearNote: Date not given in BAWS.
summary: A short foreword praising a book on commodity exchanges in India and its link to agriculture.
whyItMatters: A small example of Ambedkar supporting other Indian economists' work.

title: Foreword to "Social Insurance and India" by M. R. Idgunji
yearNote: Date not given in BAWS.
summary: A short foreword to a book on social insurance such as workmen's compensation.
whyItMatters: Shows his interest in social security for workers, which he later pursued as Labour Member.

title: Evidence before the Southborough Committee on Franchise
yearNote: Written statement and oral examination on 27 January 1919 (Reforms Committee (Franchise) Report, Vol. II, 1919).
summary: Ambedkar told a British committee planning new voting rules that "untouchable" Hindus formed a separate social group from "touchable" Hindus. He asked for separate representation so that they could speak for themselves in the legislatures.
whyItMatters: It was his first public political demand for the political rights of the untouchables.

title: Speeches in the Bombay Legislative Council and Assembly (1927–1939)
yearNote: From his maiden budget speech of 24 February 1927 to the war debates of October 1939.
summary: Forty-seven speeches as a nominated member (from February 1927) and later as an elected member of the Bombay legislature. They cover budgets, education, the Mahar watan system, the Khoti land system, police powers, prohibition, maternity benefits and workers' strikes.
whyItMatters: They show him as a working legislator fighting for peasants, workers and the depressed classes through law.

title: Bill No. XX of 1937 to Abolish the Khoti System
yearNote: Introduced in the Bombay Legislative Assembly, 17 September 1937.
summary: A private bill drafted by Ambedkar to end the "khoti" system in the Konkan, under which landlords collected rent from tenant farmers and could exploit them. He spoke for it the same day.
whyItMatters: It was one of the first attempts in India to abolish a landlord system by law.

title: Bills to Amend the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act (Mahar Watan)
yearNote: Bill No. XII of 1928 (19 March 1928) and Bill No. XXIII of 1937 (17 September 1937).
summary: Bills to free Mahar village servants from the "watan" system, which tied them to unpaid or badly paid hereditary village duties in return for small plots of land.
whyItMatters: They tackled one of the economic roots of untouchability in Maharashtra.

title: Written Evidence to the Bombay University Reforms Committee
yearNote: Printed as Appendix III in BAWS Vol. 2; date not stated in the contents.
summary: Ambedkar's answers to a questionnaire about reforming the University of Bombay, including how education could reach backward communities.
whyItMatters: It shows his lifelong belief that higher education was key to the rise of the depressed classes.

title: Report on the Constitution of the Government of Bombay Presidency (Views and Recommendations to the Indian Statutory Commission)
yearNote: Prepared as a member of the Bombay Provincial Committee that worked with the Simon Commission; Pritchett dates it to 1929.
summary: Ambedkar wrote his own report for the committee working with the Simon Commission. He recommended adult franchise, reserved seats for the depressed classes, and more powers for elected ministers.
whyItMatters: It is an early, detailed plan for a democratic constitution written by an Indian.

title: Statement concerning the State of Education of the Depressed Classes in the Bombay Presidency
yearNote: Submitted on behalf of the Bahishkrita Hitakarini Sabha to the Indian Statutory Commission, 29 May 1928.
summary: Using official numbers, this memorandum shows how few children of the depressed classes were in school and college, and asks for scholarships, hostels and special help.
whyItMatters: It is a data-based case for educational justice.

title: Statement concerning the Safeguards for the Protection of the Interests of the Depressed Classes as a Minority
yearNote: Submitted on behalf of the Bahishkrita Hitakarini Sabha to the Indian Statutory Commission, 29 May 1928.
summary: A memorandum arguing that the depressed classes were a minority needing legal protection, including representation in legislatures and in government jobs.
whyItMatters: It set out the case for the safeguards he would fight for at the Round Table Conferences.

title: Evidence before the Indian Statutory Commission (Simon Commission)
yearNote: Oral evidence, 23 October 1928.
summary: Ambedkar was questioned by the Simon Commission about the condition and political rights of the depressed classes.
whyItMatters: It brought the depressed classes' case directly before the British commission reviewing India's constitution.

title: Note Submitted to the Indian Franchise Committee (Lothian Committee)
summary: A note to the British committee deciding who should get the vote under the new constitution, written from the point of view of the depressed classes.
whyItMatters: It shows him pressing for wide voting rights for the poor.

title: Speeches at the Round Table Conferences, London (1930–1931)
yearNote: First session November 1930 – January 1931; second session September – December 1931.
summary: Ambedkar represented the depressed classes at the conferences in London on India's future constitution. He spoke in the plenary sessions and in committees on federal structure, provinces, minorities, franchise, defence and services.
whyItMatters: For the first time the untouchables had their own voice at the table where India's constitution was being planned.

title: A Scheme of Political Safeguards for the Protection of the Depressed Classes in the Future Constitution of a Self-Governing India
yearNote: Memorandum by Dr. Ambedkar and Rao Bahadur R. Srinivasan, appended to the report of the Minorities Sub-Committee, first Round Table Conference (1930–31).
summary: A list of demands for the depressed classes in a new constitution: equal citizenship, laws against social boycott, fair representation in legislatures and services, and special care in education.
whyItMatters: Many of these ideas later appeared in India's Constitution, such as the abolition of untouchability.

title: Supplementary Memorandum on the Claims of the Depressed Classes for Special Representation
yearNote: By Dr. Ambedkar and Rao Bahadur R. Srinivasan, Minorities Committee, second Round Table Conference (1931).
summary: A follow-up memorandum spelling out how many seats the depressed classes should get and asking for separate electorates.
whyItMatters: It was the basis of the dispute with Gandhi that led to the Poona Pact of 1932.

title: Claims of Minority Communities – Joint Memorandum (Minorities Pact)
yearNote: Joint memorandum of several minority delegations, second Round Table Conference, 1931.
summary: A joint statement by Muslim, depressed-class, Indian Christian, Anglo-Indian and European delegates setting out their common claims for protection.
whyItMatters: It shows the alliance of minorities that Ambedkar joined at the conference.

title: Evidence before the Joint Committee on Indian Constitutional Reform (questions to witnesses)
yearNote: June–November 1933, London; he examined witnesses including Winston Churchill (24–25 October 1933) and Sir Samuel Hoare.
summary: As a member of the British Parliament's Joint Committee on the new Indian constitution, Ambedkar cross-examined many witnesses, including on the Poona Pact.
whyItMatters: It shows him questioning powerful British politicians about India's future.

title: Annihilation of Caste
altTitles: Annihilation of Caste with a Reply to Mahatma Gandhi
yearNote: Written as the presidential address for the 1936 annual conference of the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal, Lahore, which was never delivered; Ambedkar published it himself in 1936. Second edition 1937 (with Gandhi's articles and Ambedkar's reply); third edition 1944. BAWS reprints the 1944 text.
summary: Ambedkar was invited to give a speech against caste in Lahore, but the organisers backed out when they read his text. He printed it himself. In it he argues that caste cannot be ended by small reforms, because it rests on religious beliefs in the Hindu scriptures, and that real change needs liberty, equality and fraternity.
whyItMatters: It is his most famous essay and one of the most important attacks on the caste system ever written. It started a public debate with Gandhi.

online.label: Columbia University (CCNMTL / Frances Pritchett) – annotated e-text for students
Internet Archive – 1944/1945 third edition scan (Digital Library of India)

title: Maharashtra as a Linguistic Province
yearNote: Statement submitted to the Linguistic Provinces Commission; published 1948.
summary: A statement to the government commission studying states based on language. Ambedkar supports a Marathi-speaking province and argues, point by point, against the claim that the city of Bombay should be kept out of Maharashtra.
whyItMatters: It was an early, reasoned case in the debate that led to the creation of Maharashtra state with Bombay in 1960.

title: Need for Checks and Balances
yearNote: The Times of India, 23 April 1953.
summary: A newspaper article about states formed on the basis of language. Ambedkar warns that in such states one big caste or community could dominate smaller communities, so the constitution must include protections.
whyItMatters: It shows that he supported linguistic states but worried about the safety of minorities and the untouchables inside them.

title: Thoughts on Linguistic States
yearNote: First published 1955.
summary: Written in response to the report of the States Reorganisation Commission, this short book accepts "one state, one language" but warns against very large states. Ambedkar proposes dividing Uttar Pradesh into three states and suggests that India needs a second capital to ease tension between North and South.
whyItMatters: Many of the questions he raised about state size and the North–South balance are still debated today.

online.label: Internet Archive – scan

title: Ranade, Gandhi and Jinnah
yearNote: Address on the 101st birthday of M. G. Ranade, Gokhale Memorial Hall, Poona, 18 January 1943; published 1943.
summary: A speech in honour of the social reformer Mahadev Govind Ranade. Ambedkar praises Ranade's commitment to social reform and criticises the blind hero-worship he saw around Gandhi and Jinnah.
whyItMatters: It explains what Ambedkar thought makes a great man, and why he valued social reform over political slogans.

online.label: Columbia University (Frances Pritchett) – full text of the 1943 edition

title: Federation versus Freedom
yearNote: Kale Memorial Lecture, Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics, Poona, 29 January 1939; published as "Tracts for the Times No. 3".
summary: A lecture examining the federal scheme in the Government of India Act, 1935. Ambedkar argues that the plan, which joined British provinces with princely states, would not bring India real freedom or responsible government.
whyItMatters: It shows his deep knowledge of constitutions years before he chaired the drafting of India's own.

online.label: Internet Archive – 1939 edition scan (Digital Library of India)

title: Communal Deadlock and a Way to Solve It
yearNote: Address at the session of the All India Scheduled Castes Federation, Bombay, 6 May 1945; published 1945.
summary: A proposal for sharing seats in the legislature among India's communities. Ambedkar argues that "majority rule" by one community is unjust: a majority community may have more seats than others, but never an absolute majority on its own.
whyItMatters: It was his plan to break the political deadlock between communities just before independence.

title: States and Minorities: What Are Their Rights and How to Secure Them in the Constitution of Free India
yearNote: Memorandum on behalf of the All India Scheduled Castes Federation to the Constituent Assembly; published 1947.
summary: Written as a model constitution for a "United States of India", it lists fundamental rights, protections for the Scheduled Castes, and an economic plan. It proposes state ownership of agriculture and key industries ("State Socialism") to prevent great inequality.
whyItMatters: It shows the kind of constitution Ambedkar wanted before he became chairman of the Drafting Committee.

title: Philosophy of Hinduism
yearNote: Undated typescript found among his papers; first published in BAWS Vol. 3 (1987).
summary: Ambedkar puts Hinduism "on trial" by asking whether its rules, especially those in the Manu Smriti, are fair to all people. He judges religion by the standards of justice and usefulness to society and concludes that Hinduism, as laid down in its law books, fails them.
whyItMatters: It is one of his deepest discussions of religion and morality, and it shaped his later turn to Buddhism.

yearNote: Unfinished at his death; a letter of June 1956 to S. S. Rege (facsimile in BAWS Vol. 3) shows he was still working on it. Chapters first published 1987.

yearNote: Undated manuscript with corrections in his handwriting; first published in BAWS Vol. 4 (Government of Maharashtra, 1987). BAWS Vol. 3's introduction counts 26 "Riddles" titles among his papers plus one from S. S. Rege.

title: Pakistan or the Partition of India
yearNote: First published December 1940 as "Thoughts on Pakistan"; second edition February 1945 and third edition 1946 under the title "Pakistan or the Partition of India" (Thacker & Co., Bombay). BAWS reprints the 1946 edition.

summary: Sixty-eight speeches and statements made while Ambedkar was Labour Member (minister for labour) in the British Government of India. title: Labour and Parliamentary Democracy
yearNote: Speech at the concluding session of the All India Trade Union Workers' Study Camp, Delhi (8–17 September 1943); published by the Indian Federation of Labour.

yearNote: From 17 December 1946 to 26 November 1949.
summary: All of Ambedkar's speeches in the body that wrote India's Constitution, including his first speech on the Objectives Resolution, his introduction of the Draft Constitution, his replies on each article, and his final speech before adoption.
whyItMatters: As chairman of the Drafting Committee he explained and defended almost every part of the Constitution.

yearNote: Covering letter dated 21 February 1948; Draft published in the Gazette of India, 26 February 1948.
summary: The first full draft of India's Constitution prepared by the Drafting Committee under Ambedkar's chairmanship, with his letter to Dr. Rajendra Prasad explaining the main choices.
whyItMatters: It is the text that the Constituent Assembly debated article by article in 1948–49.

title: The Hindu Code Bill (draft and speeches)
yearNote: Debated from 17 November 1947 to 25 September 1951.
summary: Ambedkar's draft Hindu Code and his speeches as Law Minister for it. The Bill set out to codify Hindu law on property, succession, maintenance, marriage, divorce, adoption and guardianship. It gave women rights to inherit property, allowed divorce and made monogamy the rule.
whyItMatters: It was his biggest attempt to bring equality into family life. Its failure to pass in 1951 was one of the reasons he gave for resigning from the Cabinet.

title: Statement in Explanation of His Resignation from the Cabinet

whyItMatters: It is his frank account of his time as independent India's first Law Minister.

yearNote: Compilation of Buddhist prayers printed in Devanagari script; BAWS Vol. 16 (1998) prints it as Book IV. BAWS does not give the year of its first separate printing (it is often dated 1956), and the exact mix of Pali and Marathi was not checked.

whyItMatters: It gave the new converts a common form of worship.

title: Mahad Satyagraha: Speeches and Documents (1927)
yearNote: March and December 1927.
summary: Reports, speeches and documents about the struggle at Mahad (Kolaba district) to use the Chavdar Tank, a public water tank, and the December 1927 conference at which the Manu Smriti was burnt. Ambedkar compared the conference to the French National Assembly of 1789.
whyItMatters: Mahad was the first great mass action by the untouchables for civil rights.

title: Kalaram Temple Entry Satyagraha, Nasik, and the Temple Entry Movement (documents)
summary: Reports and statements about the campaign to let untouchables enter the Kalaram temple in Nasik, and about the wider temple-entry movement.
whyItMatters: It shows why Ambedkar later said that political power and education mattered more than temple entry.

title: A Bill to Control and Regulate Money-Lending
yearNote: Private bill, Bombay Legislative Assembly (BAWS gives no exact date).
summary: A draft law to protect poor borrowers from moneylenders by controlling interest and requiring licences and accounts.
whyItMatters: It shows his concern for indebted peasants and workers.

title: Representation Relating to the Grievances of the Watandar Mahars, Mangs etc.
yearNote: Linked in BAWS (citing Keer) to the conference of Watandar Mahars and Mangs at Haregaon, Ahmednagar district, in December 1939.
summary: A petition to the Bombay Government against new taxes on the Mahar watan lands held by village servants.
whyItMatters: Part of his long fight against the watan system that tied Mahars to village service.

title: Dr. Ambedkar and the Jewish People (interview)
yearNote: Interview with the editor of "The Jewish Advocate", Bombay, November 1941.
summary: An interview in which Ambedkar praised the Jewish settlers in Palestine for the social order they were building.
whyItMatters: It is a rare record of his views on another persecuted people.

title: Scheduled Castes' Emancipation – Draft Election Manifesto of the All India Scheduled Castes Federation
yearNote: Decided at a meeting at his New Delhi residence on 6 October 1951 (BAWS, citing Khairmode).
summary: The manifesto for India's first general election, setting out the Federation's programme for the Scheduled Castes and for the country.
whyItMatters: It shows his political programme after leaving the Cabinet.

title: Letter to Jawaharlal Nehru regarding "The Buddha and His Dhamma"
yearNote: 14 September 1956.
summary: A letter telling Prime Minister Nehru that the book was finished and in the press, and asking whether the Government of India could buy copies, because the printing cost (about Rs. 20,000) was beyond his means.
whyItMatters: It shows how close to finished the book was a few weeks before the conversion of October 1956.

title: Thoughts on the Reform of Legal Education in the Bombay Presidency
yearNote: Government Law College Magazine, Vol. VII, No. 1, January 1936 (written as Principal of the College).
summary: Written while he was Principal of the Government Law College, Bombay, this article proposes changes to how lawyers are trained, such as practical training in chambers.
whyItMatters: It shows him as an educator shaping the legal profession.

title: Dr. Ambedkar's Reply to Sir S. Radhakrishnan
yearNote: Published in "The Lamp", 25 June 1936 (BAWS, quoting Khairmode).
summary: A short reply to the philosopher S. Radhakrishnan's argument that the survival of Hinduism over the ages proved its greatness.
whyItMatters: It belongs to the 1936 debate after he announced he would leave Hinduism.

title: Foreword to "Untouchable Workers of Bombay City" by G. R. Pradhan
yearNote: Dated Rajgrih, Dadar, 10 February 1938 (Karnatak Publishing House, Bombay, 1938).
summary: A foreword to a survey of the living and working conditions of untouchable workers in Bombay.
whyItMatters: It shows his support for social research on workers.

title: Is Gandhi a Mahatma?
yearNote: Originally published in "Chitra" (Marathi), Diwali special number, 1938 (BAWS note).
summary: A sharp article saying that Ambedkar distrusts all "Mahatmas" and arguing that Gandhi's teaching did not help the untouchables.
whyItMatters: It shows the depth of his disagreement with Gandhi.

title: Preface to "The Essence of Buddhism" by P. Lakshmi Narasu (third edition)
yearNote: Dated 10 March 1948; third edition published 1948 by Thacker & Co., Bombay.
summary: Ambedkar's preface to a reprint of Prof. P. Lakshmi Narasu's book on Buddhism, praising Narasu as a social reformer who fought caste.
whyItMatters: He chose to republish this book as his interest in Buddhism grew.

title: Buddha and the Future of His Religion
yearNote: Maha Bodhi (journal of the Maha Bodhi Society, Calcutta), Vaishakh Number, Vol. 58, May 1950.
summary: Ambedkar compares the Buddha with Jesus, Muhammad and Krishna, and argues that the Buddha's teaching, based on reason and morality, is the religion best suited to the modern world. He suggests practical steps to spread Buddhism.
whyItMatters: It is a key public statement of his choice of Buddhism, six years before his conversion.

title: The Rise and Fall of the Hindu Woman: Who Was Responsible for It?
yearNote: Maha Bodhi, May–June 1951, Vol. 59, pp. 137–151 (BAWS footnote). It replies to an article in Eve's Weekly (21 January 1950).
summary: Ambedkar answers a magazine article that blamed the Buddha for the decline of Indian women. He argues that the Buddha raised women's status, and that the Manu Smriti was responsible for their fall.
whyItMatters: It is one of his main writings on women and religion.

title: A People at Bay (outline)
yearNote: Undated outline of a planned book.
summary: The table of contents of a planned book about the untouchables, including chapters on whether they should stay within Hinduism.
whyItMatters: Another book he planned but did not write.

title: The Mahars: Who Were They and How They Became the Untouchables?
yearNote: Untitled manuscript; title supplied by the editors.
summary: An unfinished paper on the history of the Mahar community of Maharashtra, to which Ambedkar belonged.
whyItMatters: It applies his theory of untouchability to his own community.

title: Memorandum Submitted to the Cabinet Mission
yearNote: 1946 (BAWS, citing Keer).
summary: The All-India Scheduled Castes Federation's demands to the British Cabinet Mission about how the Scheduled Castes should be protected in a free India.
whyItMatters: It is the official statement of the Scheduled Castes' case in 1946.

title: India and the British Commonwealth (note)
yearNote: November 1948 (BAWS prints it after a letter to him dated 19 November 1948 from the Finance Minister).
summary: A note on whether and how a republican India should stay linked to the British Commonwealth.
whyItMatters: It shows his advice on a big foreign-policy choice made in 1949.

title: Constitution and Constitutionalism: The Constitution of India – An Exposition of Its Principles
yearNote: Undated, unfinished; written after the Constitution was adopted (1949).
summary: The beginning of a planned book explaining the principles of India's new Constitution and comparing it with other constitutions.
whyItMatters: It is the start of his own commentary on the Constitution he helped write.

title: Mooknayak (मूकनायक – "Leader of the Voiceless")
yearNote: First issue 31 January 1920. Fortnightly, Marathi, Bombay (Parel). The last surviving issue is No. 19 of 23 October 1920; some sources say the paper continued until 1922 or 1923. Pritchett's timeline calls it a weekly; issue dates support fortnightly.
summary: Ambedkar's first newspaper, started with Rs. 2,500 from Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur. Because he was then a college professor, others were named as editor (first P. N. Bhatkar, then D. D. Gholap), but Ambedkar wrote its early editorials before leaving for London in July 1920. Its masthead carried verses of the saint Tukaram.
whyItMatters: It was the first paper through which the untouchables of Maharashtra spoke for themselves.

title: Bahishkrit Bharat (बहिष्कृत भारत – "Excluded India")
yearNote: First issue 3 April 1927; fortnightly (Fridays) from issue 2; last issue (joint no. 21–22) dated 15 November 1929 according to the 1990 reprint. Forward Press, citing Vasant Moon, gives 19 November 1929.

whyItMatters: Its editorials are among his most powerful Marathi writings.

title: Samata (समता – "Equality")
yearNote: Launched 29 June 1928; fortnightly; closed after 19 issues in March 1929 (Ashok Gopal, via The News Minute). Forward Press gives a different start date in one place.
summary: The paper of the Samaj Samata Sangh (Social Equality League), issued under Ambedkar's leadership but edited by Devrao Naik; Ambedkar himself did not write for it. Each editorial carried the "Golden Rule" from the Mahabharata and the Bible.
whyItMatters: It was an experiment in getting caste Hindus to write against caste.

title: Janata (जनता – "The People")
yearNote: First issue 24 November 1930 (EPW; Forward Press gives 25 November). Weekly. Renamed Prabuddha Bharat on 4 February 1956.
summary: The longest-running paper of Ambedkar's movement, published under his guidance from 1930 until 1956. Editors included Devrao Naik, Bhaskarrao Kadrekar, Gangadhar Sahastrabuddhe and later B. C. Kamble; Ambedkar did not hold the editor's title.
whyItMatters: It recorded his speeches and campaigns for a quarter of a century.

title: Original thesis manuscript lost at sea (1917)
yearNote: Lost in 1917 when the steamer carrying his belongings back to India was torpedoed (Keer, via Pritchett).

whyItMatters: It shows how much he had to redo to finish his London degrees after returning in 1920.
